chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is the province of a magnanimous man to bear with mildness the errors of others.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 12, pp. 47–48.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is comely not to oppose the law, nor a prince, nor one wiser than yourself.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 13, pp. 48.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: A good man pays no attention to the reproofs of the depraved.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 14, pp. 48.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is hard to be governed by those who are worse than ourselves.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 15, pp. 48.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: He who is perfectly vanquished by riches, can never be just.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 16, pp. 48.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Reason is frequently more persuasive than gold itself.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 17, pp. 48.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: He who admonishes a man that fancies he has intellect, labours in vain.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 18, pp. 49.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Many who have not learnt to argue rationally, still live according to reason.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 19, pp. 49.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Many who commit the basest actions often exercise the best discourse.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 20, pp. 49.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Fools frequently become wise under the pressure of misfortunes.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 21, pp. 49.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is necessary to emulate the works and actions, and not the words of virtue.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 22, pp. 49.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Those who are naturally well disposed know things beautiful, and are themselves emulous of them.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 23, pp. 49–50.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Vigour and strength of body are the nobility of cattle; but rectitude of manners is the nobility of man.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 24, pp. 50.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The hopes of Wise Men may come to pass, but those of Fools are impossible.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Neither art nor wisdom can be acquired without preparatory learning.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 25, pp. 50.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is better to reprove your own errors, than those of others.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 26, pp. 50.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Those whose manners are well ordered, will also be orderly in their lives.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 27, pp. 50.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is good not only to refrain from doing an injury, but even from the very wish.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 28, pp. 50–51.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is proper to speak well of good works; for to do so of such as are base is the property of a fraudulent man and an impostor.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 29, pp. 51.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Many that have great learning have no intellect.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 30, pp. 51.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is necessary to endeavour to obtain an abundance of intellect, and not pursue an abundance of erudition.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 31, pp. 51.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is better that counsel should precede actions, than that repentance should follow them.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 32, pp. 51.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Put not confidence in all men, but in those that are worthy; for to do the former is the province of a stupid man, but the latter of a wise man.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 33, pp. 52.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: A worthy and an unworthy man are to be judged not from their actions only, but also from their will.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 34, pp. 52.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: To desire immoderately is the province of a boy, and not of a man.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 35, pp. 52.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Unseasonable pleasures bring forth pains.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 36, pp. 52.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Vehement desires about any one thing render the soul blind with respect to other things.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 37, pp. 52.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The love is just which, unattended with injury, aspires after things becoming.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 38, pp. 53.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Admit nothing as pleasant which is not advantageous.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 39, pp. 53.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is better for the Unwise to be Governed, than to Govern.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Not argument but calamity is the preceptor to children.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 41, pp. 53.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Glory and wealth without wisdom are not secure possessions.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 42, pp. 53.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is not indeed useless to procure wealth, but to procure it from injustice is the most pernicious of all things.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 43, pp. 53–54.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is a dreadful thing to imitate the bad, and to be unwilling to imitate the good.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 44, pp. 54.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is a shameful thing for a man to be employed about the affairs of others, but to be ignorant of his own.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 45, pp. 54.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: To be always intending to act renders action imperfect.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 46, pp. 54.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Fraudulent men, and such as are only seemingly good, do all things in words and nothing in deeds.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 47, pp. 54.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The ignorance of what is excellent is the cause of error.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 49, pp. 55.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Prior to the performance of base things, a man should reverence himself.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 50, pp. 55.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: A man given to contradiction, and very attentive to trifles, is naturally unadapted to learn what is proper.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 51, pp. 55.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Continually to speak without being willing to hear, is arrogance.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 52, pp. 55.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is necessary to guard against a depraved man, lest he should take advantage of opportunity.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 53, pp. 56.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: An envious man is the cause of molestation to himself, as to an enemy.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 54, pp. 56.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Not only he is an enemy who acts unjustly, but even he who deliberates about so acting.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 55, pp. 56.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The enmity of relations is far more bitter than that of strangers.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 56, pp. 56.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Conduct yourself to all men without suspicion; and be accommodating and cautious in your behaviour.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 57, pp. 56.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is proper to receive favours, at the same time determining that the retribution shall surpass the gift.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 58, pp. 57.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: When about to bestow a favour, previously consider him who is to receive it, lest being a fraudulent character he should return evil for good.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 59, pp. 57.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Small favours seasonably bestowed, become things of the greatest consequence to those that receive them.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 60, pp. 57.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Honours, with wise men, are capable of effecting the greatest things, if at the same time they understand that they are honoured.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 61, pp. 57.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The beneficent man is one who does not look to retribution; but who deliberately intends to do well.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 62, pp. 58.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Many that appear to be friends are not, and others, who do not appear to be friends, are so.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 63, pp. 58.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The friendship of one wise man is better than that of every fool.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 64, pp. 58.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: He is unworthy to live, who has not one worthy friend.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 65, pp. 58.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Many turn from their friends, if, from affluence, they fall into adversity.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 66, pp. 58.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The equal is beautiful in every thing; but excess and defect to me do not appear to be so.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 67, pp. 59.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: He who loves no one does not appear to me to be loved by any one.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 68, pp. 59.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: He is an agreeable old man who is facetious, and abounds in interesting anecdote.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 69, pp. 59.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The beauty of the body is merely animal unless supported by intellect.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 70, pp. 59.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: To find a friend in prosperity, is very easy; but in adversity, it is the most difficult of all things.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 71, pp. 59.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Not all relations are friends, but those who accord with what is mutually advantageous.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 72, pp. 60.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Since we are men, it is becoming not to deride, but bewail, the calamities of men.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 73, pp. 60.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Good scarcely presents itself, even to those who investigate it; but evil is obvious without investigation.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 74, pp. 60.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Men who delight to blame others are not naturally adapted to friendship.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 75, pp. 60.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: A woman should not be given to loquacity; for it is a dreadful thing.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 76, pp. 60.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: To be governed by a woman is the extremity of insolence and unmanliness.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 77, pp. 61.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is the property of a divine intellect to be always intently thinking about the beautiful.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 78, pp. 61.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Those who praise the unwise do them a great injury.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 80, pp. 61.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is better to be praised by another than by oneself.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 81, pp. 62.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: If you cannot reconcile to yourself the praises you receive, think that you are flattered.
chunks.credit: William Bridgman · Translations from the Greek (London: printed for W. Bridgman by R. Wilks, 1804), The Golden Sentences of Democrates, sentence 82, pp. 62.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: I came to Athens and no one knew me.
chunks.credit: R. D. Hicks · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, vol. II (Loeb Classical Library, 1925)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Of a truth we know nothing, for truth is in a well.
chunks.credit: R. D. Hicks · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, vol. II (Loeb Classical Library, 1925)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: For instance, Democritus himself, as the story goes, used to say that he would rather discover one single law of causation than receive the kingdom of Persia, and this, although he was vainly seeking causes where no cause was, as one who started from a false principle and an erroneous hypothesis, and did not discern the root and the necessity common to the nature of all things, but regarded the contemplation of senseless and random contingencies as the highest wisdom, and set up chance as the mistress and queen of
chunks.credit: E. H. Gifford · Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1903)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: all things, but regarded the contemplation of senseless and random contingencies as the highest wisdom, and set up chance as the mistress and queen of things universal and things divine, and declared that all things took place in accordance therewith, but banished it from the life of man, and convicted those who worshipped it as senseless.
chunks.credit: E. H. Gifford · Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1903)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: For example, in the beginning of his Suggestions he says: "Men formed an image of chance as an excuse for their own folly: for chance is by nature antagonistic to judgement: and this worst enemy of wisdom they said ruled over it; or rather they utterly overthrow and annihilate this latter, and set up the other in its place: for they praise not wisdom as fortunate, but fortune as most wise."
chunks.credit: E. H. Gifford · Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1903)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: as Democritus said, words are but the shadows of actions.
chunks.credit: Simon Ford; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 1 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: his reason looks inward and is well rooted within him, and that the man (as Democritus said) is accustomed to take satisfaction from himself.
chunks.credit: Mr. Tod; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 2 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is absurd, as Democritus says, by the croaking of ravens, the crowing of a cock, or the wallowing of a sow in the mire, carefully to observe the signs of windy or rainy weather, and not to prevent and guard ourselves against the motions and fluctuations of our bodies or the indication of a distemper, nor to understand the signs of a storm which is just ready to break forth within ourselves.
chunks.credit: Matthew Poole; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 1 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: for the navel as Democritus says, grows first, like an anchor to keep the foetus from fluctuating, or as a stay or footstalk to the child
chunks.credit: R. Brown; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 4 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Let us then say also to ourselves: Thy body, O man, naturally of itself breeds many diseases and passions, and many it receives befalling it from without; but if thou shalt open thy interior, thou wilt find a certain various and abundantly furnished storehouse and (as Democritus says) treasury of evils, not flowing into it from abroad, but having as it were their inbred and original springs, which vice, exceedingly affluent and rich in passions, causes to break forth.
chunks.credit: S. White; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 4 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: thus light and easy disquisitions do pleasantly and profitably excite us, but we must forbear all contentious and (to use Democritus’s word) wrangling disputes,
chunks.credit: T. C.; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 3 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: for in a fish eaten in common, Democritus says, there are no bones.
chunks.credit: T. C.; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 3 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Lightning is wonderfully piercing and subtile, partly because it rises from a very pure substance, and partly because by the swiftness of its motion it purges itself and throws off all gross earthy particles that are mixed with it. Nothing, says Democritus, is blasted with lightning, that cannot resist and stop the motion of the pure flame.
chunks.credit: T. C.; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 3 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Lightning is wonderfully piercing and subtile, partly because it rises from a very pure substance, and partly because by the swiftness of its motion it purges itself and throws off all gross earthy particles that are mixed with it.
chunks.credit: T. C.; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 3 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Nothing, says Democritus, is blasted with lightning, that cannot resist and stop the motion of the pure flame.
chunks.credit: T. C.; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 3 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

context.text: Lightning is wonderfully piercing and subtile, partly because it rises from a very pure substance, and partly because by the swiftness of its motion it purges itself and throws off all gross earthy particles that are mixed with it. Nothing, says Democritus, is blasted with lightning, that cannot resist and stop the motion of the pure flame.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: since a wise statesman will not despise true honor and favor, consisting in the good-will and friendly disposition of those who gratefully remember his services; nor will he contemn glory by shunning to please his neighbors, as Democritus would have him.
chunks.credit: Samuel White; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 5 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: But perhaps we may seem ridiculous for signalizing beasts in this manner because they learn, since we find that Democritus affirms us to have been their scholars in the greatest matters;—of the spider, in weaving and repairing what we tear or wear out; of the swallow, in building houses; and of the mournful swan and nightingale, in singing and imitation.
chunks.credit: John Philips; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 5 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: See it yet farther, in what manner he answered Democritus, enquiring philosophically and properly, if a cone is divided by a plane parallel with its base, what is to be thought of the superficies of its segments, whether they are equal or unequal; for if they are unequal, they will render the cone uneven, receiving many step-like incisions and roughnesses; but if they are equal, the sections will be equal, and the cone will seem to have the same qualities as the cylinder, to wit, to be composed not of
chunks.credit: S. White; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 4 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: the sections will be equal, and the cone will seem to have the same qualities as the cylinder, to wit, to be composed not of unequal but of equal circles; which is most absurd.
chunks.credit: S. White; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 4 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Now the first thing he lays to his charge is, that, by supposing every thing to be no more of one nature than another, he wholly confounds human life. But Democritus was so far from having been of this opinion, that he opposed Protagoras the philosopher who asserted it, and writ many excellent arguments concluding against him, which this fine fellow Colotes never saw nor read, nor yet so much as dreamed of; but deceived himself by misunderstanding a passage which is in his works, where he determines that τὸ
chunks.credit: A. G.; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 5 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: read, nor yet so much as dreamed of; but deceived himself by misunderstanding a passage which is in his works, where he determines that τὸ δέν is no more than τὸ μηδέν, naming in that place the body by δέν, and the void by μηδέν, and meaning that the void has its own proper nature and subsistence, as well as the body.
chunks.credit: A. G.; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 5 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Now the first thing he lays to his charge is, that, by supposing every thing to be no more of one nature than another, he wholly confounds human life.
chunks.credit: A. G.; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 5 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

context.text: Now the first thing he lays to his charge is, that, by supposing every thing to be no more of one nature than another, he wholly confounds human life. But Democritus was so far from having been of this opinion, that he opposed Protagoras the philosopher who asserted it, and writ many excellent arguments concluding against him, which this fine

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Amongst whom, Democritus in his writings advises and exhorts to the learning of political science, as being the greatest of all, and to the accustoming one’s self to bear fatigues, by which men attain to great wealth and honor.
chunks.credit: A. G.; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 5 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: and, as Democritus tells us, men setting themselves every new-spring day to endeavors of mutual beneficence and service one towards another, as if they were fastened in the straitest tie together, do all of them, some from one, some from another quarter of the world, rouse up and awake to action.
chunks.credit: Charles Whitaker; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 3 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: To such as these I think Democritus chiefly spoke, when he said, that if the body should summon the soul before a court on an action for ill-treatment, the soul would lose the case.
chunks.credit: Matthew Poole; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 1 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The bounds of profitable and unprofitable are, pleasant and unpleasant.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is easy to praise what we ought not, and to blame; but both are signs of a depraved disposition.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is the work of Prudence to prevent an injury; of Indolence, when done, not to revenge it.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: There ariseth a great delight from beholding good actions.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Temperance augments things that are pleasant, and maketh the pleasure it self greater.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Sleeps in the day signifieth either distemper of the Body, or grief of the Mind, or sloth, or dulness.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Not he only is valiant who vanquisheth his Enemy, but he also who subdueth Pleasure; yet some there are, who Command Cities, and are slaves to Women.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Wisdom not admiring any thing, merits all things, being most Honourable.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Those alone are dear to divinity, who are hostile to injustice.
chunks.credit: Thomas Taylor · Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagoras, or Pythagoric Life (London: A. J. Valpy, 1818), appendix Pythagoric Ethical Sentences from Stobæus, p. 262.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Where ill Actions acquire Wealth, the Infamy is the greater.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Hope of ill gain is the beginning of loss.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Those things which the body necessarily requires, are easily to be procured by all men, without labor and molestation; but those things to the attainment of which labor and molestation are requisite, are objects of desire, not to the body, but to depraved opinion.
chunks.credit: Thomas Taylor · Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagoras, or Pythagoric Life (London: A. J. Valpy, 1818), appendix Pythagoric Ethical Sentences from Stobæus, p. 262.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: We ought to speak Truth where it is best.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Freedom of Speech is proper to generosity, but the difference of occasions render it dangerous.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: He is welldisposed who grieves not for what he hath not, and rejoyceth for what he hath.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Of pleasant things, those which we have most seldome, delight most.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: If a Man exceeds moderation, the sweetest things prove the most bitter.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: They who indulge to the pleasures of the Belly, consuming the time in eating, drinking, or wantonness; in all these there are short pleasures, which last as long as they are eating and drinking, but many griefs: For they are in a continual desire of these things, and when they have obtain’d them, the pleasure passeth away, and there is nothing in them but a momentany titillation; the pleasure is short, and they soon need the same again.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: To resist Anger is difficult, but to vanquish it is proper to an understanding Person.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: He who contends with his Superior, ends in Infamy.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Wicked Men, after they have escaped the danger, keep not the Oaths which they had made in their extremity.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: More are made good by Exercitation, than by Nature.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Neither say nor do ill, though alone; learn to stand more in awe of thy self than of others.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The Laws would not have prohibited every Man from living according to his own Will, if one were not injurious to another; for Envy causeth the beginning of Sedition.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Travelling teaches a man frugality, and the way in which he may be sufficient to himself. For bread made of milk and flour, and a bed of grass, are the sweetest remedies of hunger and labor.
chunks.credit: Thomas Taylor · Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagoras, or Pythagoric Life (London: A. J. Valpy, 1818), appendix Pythagoric Ethical Sentences from Stobæus, p. 265.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: To the wise man every land is eligible as a place of residence; for the whole world is the country of the worthy soul.
chunks.credit: Thomas Taylor · Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagoras, or Pythagoric Life (London: A. J. Valpy, 1818), appendix Pythagoric Ethical Sentences from Stobæus, p. 265.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Civil War hurts both Parties; the harm is equal to the Victor, and to the Vanquished.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: By Concord, besides other great things, War may be undertaken by Cities; without it, not.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is justice to do those things which ought to be done; Injustice not to do them, but to decline them.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: As concerning the killing and not killing of Animals, the business stands thus, Those who do, or would do injury, he who killeth is blameless; nay, such ought rather to be killed, than not.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: As it is written concerning Beasts and Serpents, that are in enmity with us, so also in my Opinion may we do with Men. According to the Laws of our Country, an Enemy may be kill’d in any part of the World, where no Law forbiddeth it; but Law forbiddeth sometimes, and they have sacred Rites, Covenants, and Oaths.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: As it is written concerning Beasts and Serpents, that are in enmity with us, so also in my Opinion may we do with Men.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Any Man that either kills with his own hand, or causeth to be killed by Command or Vote, a Thief, is to be esteemed innocent.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: They who suffer Injuries are to be defended to the utmost, and not to be despised; for this is just and good, the other unjust and ill.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: He hath the greatest part of Justice and Virtue, who Honors those that are Worthy.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Men are more mindful of Wrongs than of Benefits, and it is but just it should be so: as he who restores a Depositum, deserves no Commendation; but he who detains it, Blame and Punishment. The same case it is in a Ruler, who is chosen not to do ill, but good.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: To be naturally fitted for Command, is proper to the most excellent Persons.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Boldness is the beginning of an Action, the end is guided by Fortune.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Make use of Servants, as of the parts of your own Body; appoint to each a several Office.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: She that is belov’d, easily forgiveth the Offence of her Lover.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: A Woman is sharper-witted for mischief than a Man.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: To speak little, becomes a Woman; plain Attire adorns her.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: I approve not the having of Children; for I see the troubles of them are many and great; the Comforts and Pleasures few and small.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The begetting of Children seemeth to come from a most ancient Institution, and instinct of Nature, as is manifest even from brute Beasts, who beget young ones, though without hopes of receiving any advantage by them; As soon as they are brought forth, they feed and bring them up, and are solicitous for them even in the least things: and if they come to any hurt, they grieve at it. Such is the disposition of all Animals; how much more of Man, who hopes for a benefit from his Offspring.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: A prudent use of Money conduceth to the practice of liberality and relief of others; he that useth Money foolishly, makes it the Prey of all Men.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Poverty and Riches are the Names of Want and Sufficiency: He who wants, ought not to be called Rich; nor He who wants not, Poor.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: He is happy who is chearful, though possessing little; he unhappy who is troubled, amidst much wealth.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: A publick calamity is greater than a private, for it affords no hope of relief.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Expel by reasoning the unrestrained grief of a torpid soul.
chunks.credit: Thomas Taylor · Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagoras, or Pythagoric Life (London: A. J. Valpy, 1818), appendix Pythagoric Ethical Sentences from Stobæus, p. 266.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is the province of a wise man to bear poverty with equanimity.
chunks.credit: Thomas Taylor · Iamblichus’ Life of Pythagoras, or Pythagoric Life (London: A. J. Valpy, 1818), appendix Pythagoric Ethical Sentences from Stobæus, p. 266.

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: The hopes of Fools are beyond reason.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: It is certain, that the Old Man was once young; but whether the Young Man shall ever come to be Old, is uncertain. A good thing that is compleat, is better than that which is to come, it being uncertain.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.text: Old Age is a universal imperfection; it hath all things, and yet wants all things.
chunks.credit: Thomas Stanley · The History of Philosophy, third edition (London, 1701), Part XI, Democritus, chapter X

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Some men who do not understand the dissolution of our mortal nature, but are conscious of the misery in human existence, painfully spend their allotted period of life in confusion and fear, inventing lies about the time after they are dead.
chunks.credit: Robert Drew Hicks · R. D. Hicks, Stoic and Epicurean (New York: Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1910), p. 284

chunks.credit: R. D. Hicks · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, vol. II (Loeb Classical Library, 1925)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Democritus appropriated the Babylonian ethic discourses, for he is said to have combined with his own compositions a translation of the column of Acicarus. And you may find the distinction notified by him when he writes, “Thus says Democritus.” About himself, too, where, pluming himself on his erudition, he says, “I have roamed over the most ground of any man of my time, investigating the most remote parts. I have seen the most skies and lands, and I have heard of learned men in very great numbers.
chunks.credit: William Wilson · The Writings of Clement of Alexandria, vol. 1 (Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1867)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: time, investigating the most remote parts. I have seen the most skies and lands, and I have heard of learned men in very great numbers. And in composition no one has surpassed me; in demonstration, not even those among the Egyptians who are called Arpenodaptæ, with all of whom I lived in exile up to eighty years.” For he went to Babylon, and Persis, and Egypt, to learn from the Magi and the priests.
chunks.credit: William Wilson · The Writings of Clement of Alexandria, vol. 1 (Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1867)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: Pursue every path of life. In the market place are honours and prudent dealings, at home rest; in the country the charm of nature, and at sea profit; in a foreign country, if you have any possessions, there is fame, and if you are in want no one knows it but yourself. Are you married? Your house will be the best of houses. Do you remain unmarried? Your life is yet lighter. Children are darlings; a childless life is free from care.
chunks.credit: William Roger Paton · The Greek Anthology, vol.III, Loeb Classical Library (London: William Heinemann; New York: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1925 reprint)

chunks.author: Democritus
chunks.text: will be the best of houses. Do you remain unmarried? Your life is yet lighter. Children are darlings; a childless life is free from care. Youth is strong, and old age again is pious. Therefore there is no choice between two things, either not to be born or to die; for all in life is excellent.
chunks.credit: William Roger Paton · The Greek Anthology, vol.III, Loeb Classical Library (London: William Heinemann; New York: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1925 reprint)

chunks.author: Anaxarchus
chunks.text: “Erudition benefits greatly, and hurts greatly him who possesses it; it helps him who is worthy, and injures him who utters readily every word, and before the whole people. It is necessary to know the measure of time. For this is the end of wisdom. And those who sing at the doors, even if they sing skilfully, are not reckoned wise, but have the reputation of folly.”
chunks.credit: William Wilson · The Writings of Clement of Alexandria, vol. 1 (Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1867)

Amometus has written a work entirely devoted to the history of these people, just as Hecatæus has done in his treatise on the Hyperborei.

chunks.author: Hecataeus of Abdera
chunks.text: we find the greater part to be of opinion that the proper name of Jupiter in the Egyptian tongue is Amun … Hecataeus of Abdera saith, the Egyptians use this word when they call anybody; for that it is a term of calling. Therefore they must be of the opinion that the first God is the same with the universe; and therefore, while they invoke him who is unmanifest and hidden, and pray him to make himself manifest and known to them, they cry Amun.
chunks.credit: William Baxter; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 4 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Hecataeus of Abdera
chunks.text: They also that at Heliopolis (Sun-town) wait upon the sun never bring wine into his temple, they looking upon it as a thing indecent and unfitting to drink by daylight, while their lord and king looks on. The rest of them do indeed use it, but very sparingly. They have likewise many purgations, wherein they prohibit the use of wine, in which they study philosophy, and pass their time in learning and teaching things divine.
chunks.credit: William Baxter; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 4 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Hecataeus of Abdera
chunks.text: likewise many purgations, wherein they prohibit the use of wine, in which they study philosophy, and pass their time in learning and teaching things divine. Moreover their kings, being priests also themselves, were wont to drink it by a certain measure prescribed them in the sacred books, as Hecataeus informs us. And they began first to drink it in the reign of Psammetichus; but before that time they were not used to drink wine at all, no, nor to pour it forth in sacrifice as a thing they thought any
chunks.credit: William Baxter; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 4 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

chunks.author: Hecataeus of Abdera
chunks.text: that time they were not used to drink wine at all, no, nor to pour it forth in sacrifice as a thing they thought any way grateful to the Gods, but as the blood of those who in ancient times waged war against the Gods, from whom, falling down from heaven and mixing with the earth, they conceived vines to have first sprung; which is the reason (say they) that drunkenness renders men besides themselves and mad; they being, as it were, gorged with the blood of their ancestors.
chunks.credit: William Baxter; revised by W. W. Goodwin · Plutarch’s Essays and Miscellanies, vol. 4 (Boston: Little, Brown, 1911)

In all and every art, what the craftsman ought to say in answer to any question is written down in a popular form, and he who likes may learn. THEAETETUS: I suppose that you are referring to the precepts of Protagoras about wrestling and the other arts?

…

But how can any one who is ignorant dispute in a rational manner against him who knows? THEAETETUS: He cannot.

chunks.author: Protagoras
chunks.text: Pericles, who was called "the Olympian" because of his surpassing power of reasoning and of understanding, learned that both his sons, Paralus and Xanthippus, had passed from life. Protagoras describes his conduct in these words: "His sons were comely youths, but though they died within seven days of each other, he bore their deaths without repining. For he continued to hold to that serenity from which day by day he added greatly to his credit of being blest by Fortune and untroubled by sorrow, and to his high repute with
chunks.credit: Frank Cole Babbitt · Plutarch, Moralia, volume II, Loeb Classical Library (1928)

chunks.author: Protagoras
chunks.text: which day by day he added greatly to his credit of being blest by Fortune and untroubled by sorrow, and to his high repute with the people at large. For each and every man, as he beheld Pericles bearing his sorrows so stoutly, felt that he was high-minded and manful and his own superior, being only too well aware of what would be his own helplessness under such circumstances.
chunks.credit: Frank Cole Babbitt · Plutarch, Moralia, volume II, Loeb Classical Library (1928)

chunks.author: Protagoras
chunks.text: that he was high-minded and manful and his own superior, being only too well aware of what would be his own helplessness under such circumstances. For Pericles, immediately after the tidings about his two sons, none the less placed the garland upon his head, according to the time-honoured custom at Athens, and, clad in garb of white, harangued the people, 'taking lead in good counsel,' and inspiriting the Athenians to war."

chunks.author: Gorgias
chunks.text:
Men. And now, Socrates, what is colour?

Soc. You are outrageous, Meno, in thus plaguing a poor old man to give you an answer, when you will not take the trouble of remembering what is Gorgias’ definition of virtue.

[…]

Soc. Would you like me to answer you after the manner of Gorgias, which is familiar to you?

Men. I should like nothing better.

Soc. Do not he and you and Empedocles say that there are certain effluences of existence?

Men. Certainly.

Soc.
chunks.credit: Benjamin Jowett · Plato, The Dialogues of Plato, third edition, vol. II (Oxford University Press, 1892), pp. 34–35.

chunks.author: Gorgias
chunks.text:
Men. I should like nothing better.

Soc. Do not he and you and Empedocles say that there are certain effluences of existence?

Men. Certainly.

Soc. And passages into which and through which the effluences pass?

Men. Exactly.

Soc. And some of the effluences fit into the passages, and some of them are too small or too large?

Men. True.

Soc. And there is such a thing as sight?

Men. Yes.

Soc.
chunks.credit: Benjamin Jowett · Plato, The Dialogues of Plato, third edition, vol. II (Oxford University Press, 1892), pp. 34–35.

chunks.author: Gorgias
chunks.text:
passages, and some of them are too small or too large?

Men. True.

Soc. And there is such a thing as sight?

Men. Yes.

Soc. And now, as Pindar says, ‘read my meaning:’—colour is an effluence of form, commensurate with sight, and palpable to sense.

Men. That, Socrates, appears to me to be an admirable answer.

Soc. Why, yes, because it happens to be one which you have been in the habit of hearing: and your wit will have discovered, I suspect, that you may explain in the same way
chunks.credit: Benjamin Jowett · Plato, The Dialogues of Plato, third edition, vol. II (Oxford University Press, 1892), pp. 34–35.

chunks.author: Gorgias
chunks.text:
which you have been in the habit of hearing: and your wit will have discovered, I suspect, that you may explain in the same way the nature of sound and smell, and of many other similar phenomena.

Men. Quite true.

Soc. The answer, Meno, was in the orthodox solemn vein […]
chunks.credit: Benjamin Jowett · Plato, The Dialogues of Plato, third edition, vol. II (Oxford University Press, 1892), pp. 34–35.

chunks.text: In ceremonial oratory, intersperse your speech with bits of episodic eulogy, like Isocrates, who is always bringing some one forward for this purpose. And this is what Gorgias meant by saying that he always found something to talk about. For if he speaks of Achilles, he praises Peleus, then Aeacus, then Zeus; and in like manner the virtue of valour, describing its good results, and saying what it is like.

chunks.author: Gorgias
chunks.text: Let us take first the virtue of a man—he should know how to administer the state, and in the administration of it to benefit his friends and harm his enemies; and he must also be careful not to suffer harm himself. A woman’s virtue, if you wish to know about that, may also be easily described: her duty is to order her house, and keep what is indoors, and obey her husband.

Every age, every condition of life, young or old, male or female, bond or free, has a different virtue: there are virtues numberless, and no lack of definitions of them; for virtue is relative to the actions and ages of each of us in all that we do. And the same may be said of vice, Socrates.

chunks.text: There are the worthy sophists too—the excellent Prodicus for example, who have descanted in prose on the virtues of Heracles and other heroes;

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text:
And that wise man Prodicus delivers himself in a like strain concerning virtue in that composition of his about Heracles, which crowds have listened to. This, as far as I can recollect it, is the substance at least of what he says:

"When Heracles was emerging from boyhood into the bloom of youth, having reached that season in which the young man, now standing upon the verge of independence, shows plainly whether he will enter upon the path of virtue or of vice, he went forth into a quiet place,
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: the verge of independence, shows plainly whether he will enter upon the path of virtue or of vice, he went forth into a quiet place, and sat debating with himself which of those two paths he should pursue; and as he there sat musing, there appeared to him two women of great stature which drew nigh to him. The one was fair to look upon, frank and free by gift of nature, her limbs adorned with purity and her eyes with bashfulness; sobriety set the rhythm of her gait, and
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: frank and free by gift of nature, her limbs adorned with purity and her eyes with bashfulness; sobriety set the rhythm of her gait, and she was clad in white apparel. The other was of a different type; the fleshy softness of her limbs betrayed her nurture, while the complexion of her skin was embellished that she might appear whiter and rosier than she really was, and her figure that she might seem taller than nature made her; she stared with wide-open eyes, and the raiment wherewith she was clad
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: was, and her figure that she might seem taller than nature made her; she stared with wide-open eyes, and the raiment wherewith she was clad served but to reveal the ripeness of her bloom. With frequent glances she surveyed her person, or looked to see if others noticed her; while ever and anon she fixed her gaze upon the shadow of herself intently.
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text:
surveyed her person, or looked to see if others noticed her; while ever and anon she fixed her gaze upon the shadow of herself intently.

"Now when these two had drawn near to Heracles, she who was first named advanced at an even pace towards him, but the other, in her eagerness to outstrip her, ran forward to the youth, exclaiming, 'I see you, Heracles, in doubt and difficulty what path of life to choose; make me your friend, and I will lead you to the pleasantest road and easiest.
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: in doubt and difficulty what path of life to choose; make me your friend, and I will lead you to the pleasantest road and easiest. This I promise you: you shall taste all of life's sweets and escape all bitters. In the first place, you shall not trouble your brain with war or business; other topics shall engage your mind; your only speculation, what meat or drink you shall find agreeable to your palate; what delight of ear or eye; what pleasure of smell or touch; what darling lover's intercourse
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: or drink you shall find agreeable to your palate; what delight of ear or eye; what pleasure of smell or touch; what darling lover's intercourse shall most enrapture you; how you shall pillow your limbs in softest slumber; how cull each individual pleasure without alloy of pain; and if ever the suspicion steal upon you that the stream of joys will one day dwindle, trust me I will not lead you where you shall replenish the store by toil of body and trouble of soul. No!
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text:
one day dwindle, trust me I will not lead you where you shall replenish the store by toil of body and trouble of soul. No! others shall labour, but you shall reap the fruit of their labours; you shall withhold your hand from nought which shall bring you gain. For to all my followers I give authority and power to help themselves freely from every side.'

"Heracles hearing these words made answer: 'What, O lady, is the name you bear?'
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text:
give authority and power to help themselves freely from every side.'

"Heracles hearing these words made answer: 'What, O lady, is the name you bear?' To which she: 'Know that my friends call me Happiness, but they that hate me have their own nicknames for me, Vice and Naughtiness.'

"But just then the other of those fair women approached and spoke: 'Heracles, I too am come to you, seeing that your parents are well known to me, and in your nurture I have gauged your nature; wherefore I entertain good
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: come to you, seeing that your parents are well known to me, and in your nurture I have gauged your nature; wherefore I entertain good hope that if you choose the path which leads to me, you shall greatly bestir yourself to be the doer of many a doughty deed of noble emprise; and that I too shall be held in even higher honour for your sake, lit with the lustre shed by valorous deeds.
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: of noble emprise; and that I too shall be held in even higher honour for your sake, lit with the lustre shed by valorous deeds. I will not cheat you with preludings of pleasure, but I will relate to you the things that are according to the ordinances of God in very truth. Know then that among things that are lovely and of good report, not one have the gods bestowed upon mortal men apart from toil and pains.
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: then that among things that are lovely and of good report, not one have the gods bestowed upon mortal men apart from toil and pains. Would you obtain the favour of the gods, then must you pay these same gods service; would you be loved by your friends, you must benefit these friends; do you desire to be honoured by the state, you must give the state your aid; do you claim admiration for your virtue from all Hellas, you must strive to do some good to Hellas; do you
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: the state your aid; do you claim admiration for your virtue from all Hellas, you must strive to do some good to Hellas; do you wish earth to yield her fruits to you abundantly, to earth must you pay your court; do you seek to amass riches from your flocks and herds, on them must you bestow your labour; or is it your ambition to be potent as a warrior, able to save your friends and to subdue your foes, then must you learn the arts of war from those
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: be potent as a warrior, able to save your friends and to subdue your foes, then must you learn the arts of war from those who have the knowledge, and practise their application in the field when learned; or would you e'en be powerful of limb and body, then must you habituate limbs and body to obey the mind, and exercise yourself with toil and sweat.'
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text:
e'en be powerful of limb and body, then must you habituate limbs and body to obey the mind, and exercise yourself with toil and sweat.'

"At this point, (as Prodicus relates) Vice broke in exclaiming: 'See you, Heracles, how hard and long the road is by which yonder woman would escort you to her festal joys. But I will guide you by a short and easy road to happiness.'

"Then spoke Virtue: 'Nay, wretched one, what good thing hast thou?
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text:
joys. But I will guide you by a short and easy road to happiness.'

"Then spoke Virtue: 'Nay, wretched one, what good thing hast thou? or what sweet thing art thou acquainted with—that wilt stir neither hand nor foot to gain it? Thou, that mayest not even await the desire of pleasure, but, or ever that desire springs up, art already satiated; eating before thou hungerest, and drinking before thou thirsteth; who to eke out an appetite must invent an army of cooks and confectioners; and to whet thy thirst
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: hungerest, and drinking before thou thirsteth; who to eke out an appetite must invent an army of cooks and confectioners; and to whet thy thirst must lay down costliest wines, and run up and down in search of ice in summer-time; to help thy slumbers soft coverlets suffice not, but couches and feather-beds must be prepared thee and rockers to rock thee to rest; since desire for sleep in thy case springs not from toil but from vacuity and nothing in the world to do.
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: rock thee to rest; since desire for sleep in thy case springs not from toil but from vacuity and nothing in the world to do. Even the natural appetite of love thou forcest prematurely by every means thou mayest devise, confounding the sexes in thy service. Thus thou educatest thy friends: with insult in the night season and drowse of slumber during the precious hours of the day.
chunks.credit: Henry Graham Dakyns · Xenophon, The Memorabilia, in The Works of Xenophon (Macmillan and Co., 1897); Project Gutenberg eBook 1177.

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text: in thy service. Thus thou educatest thy friends: with insult in the night season and drowse of slumber during the precious hours of the day. Immortal, thou art cast forth from the company of gods, and by good men art dishonoured: that sweetest sound of all, the voice of praise, has never thrilled thine ears; and the fairest of all fair visions is hidden from thine eyes that have never beheld one bounteous deed wrought by thine own hand.

I heard that very argument used in the Lyceum yesterday by a wise man, Prodicus of Ceos; but the audience thought that he was talking mere nonsense, and no one could be persuaded that he was speaking the truth.

…

The youth began by asking Prodicus, In what way did he think that riches were a good and in what an evil?
chunks.credit: Benjamin Jowett · The Dialogues of Plato, third edition (1892)

chunks.author: Prodicus
chunks.text:
the truth.

…

The youth began by asking Prodicus, In what way did he think that riches were a good and in what an evil? Prodicus answered, as you did just now, that they were a good to good men and to those who knew in what way they should be employed, while to the bad and the ignorant they were an evil. The same is true, he went on to say, of all other things; men make them to be what they are themselves.
chunks.credit: Benjamin Jowett · The Dialogues of Plato, third edition (1892)

chunks.author: Antiphon the Sophist
chunks.text: . . . justice consists in not transgressing any of the ordinances of the state of which one is a citizen. A man would therefore exercise justice with most advantage to himself if in the presence of witnesses he held in esteem the laws, but in the absence of witnesses, the precepts of nature. For the precepts of the laws are adventitious, whereas those of nature are necessary, and the precepts of the laws are the product of agreement, not of growth, while those of nature are the product of
chunks.credit: Bernard P. Grenfell and Arthur S. Hunt · The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Part XI (1915), pp. 101–103, and Part XV (1922), p. 121

chunks.author: Antiphon the Sophist
chunks.text: nature are necessary, and the precepts of the laws are the product of agreement, not of growth, while those of nature are the product of growth, not of agreement. Thus in transgressing legal ordinances, whenever he is unobserved by the parties to the agreement, he is free both from shame and punishment, but not if he is observed. On the other hand, if he strain any of the innate principles of nature more than it can bear, the evil is no less, if he is unobserved by every one, nor
chunks.credit: Bernard P. Grenfell and Arthur S. Hunt · The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Part XI (1915), pp. 101–103, and Part XV (1922), p. 121

chunks.author: Antiphon the Sophist
chunks.text: any of the innate principles of nature more than it can bear, the evil is no less, if he is unobserved by every one, nor any greater, if every one sees. For the injury does not depend on opinion but on fact. All this is the object of our inquiry; because most of what is just according to law stands in opposition to nature.
chunks.credit: Bernard P. Grenfell and Arthur S. Hunt · The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Part XI (1915), pp. 101–103, and Part XV (1922), p. 121

For it is just to wrong no one when one is not oneself wronged; and he who gives testimony, even if it is true, cannot help to some extent doing a wrong; and there is a probability that he may himself subsequently be wronged: this is at any rate possible, in so far as the man against whom he testifies is convicted in consequence of

Herein therefore he wrongs the man against whom testimony is given, that he wrongs some one who is not wronging him; and he is himself wronged by such a person, because he is hated by him although he testified to the truth, and wronged not by
chunks.credit: Bernard P. Grenfell and Arthur S. Hunt · The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Part XI (1915), pp. 101–103, and Part XV (1922), p. 121

These wrongs do not seem inconsiderable, either those received or those inflicted.
chunks.credit: Bernard P. Grenfell and Arthur S. Hunt · The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Part XI (1915), pp. 101–103, and Part XV (1922), p. 121

chunks.author: Antiphon the Sophist
chunks.text: Much of what has been mentioned would be found to be in opposition to nature; there is involved in it greater pain when less is possible, or less pleasure when more is possible, or injury when injury might be avoided.

chunks.author: Antiphon the Sophist
chunks.text: Now if those who adopted such courses as these had any protection from the laws, whereas those who did not adopt them but opposed them incurred loss, obedience to the laws would not be without advantage; but as it is, legal justice is found inadequate to protect those who adopt them.

chunks.text: For it is just to wrong no one when one is not oneself wronged; and he who gives testimony, even if it is true, cannot help to some extent doing a wrong; and there is a probability that he may himself subsequently be wronged: this is at any rate possible, in so far as the man against whom he testifies is convicted in consequence of his testimony, and loses either money or life owing to a person whom he is in no way wronging.
chunks.credit: Bernard P. Grenfell and Arthur S. Hunt · The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Part XI (1915), pp. 101–103, and Part XV (1922), p. 121

chunks.author: Antiphon the Sophist
chunks.text: Herein therefore he wrongs the man against whom testimony is given, that he wrongs some one who is not wronging him; and he is himself wronged by such a person, because he is hated by him although he testified to the truth, and wronged not by his hatred only but also because he must always be on his guard against this man against whom he testified, regarding him as an enemy prepared to do what damage he can, either in word or deed.
chunks.credit: Bernard P. Grenfell and Arthur S. Hunt · The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Part XI (1915), pp. 101–103, and Part XV (1922), p. 121

In his treatise on this subject Chrysippus, just as Antipater does, has assembled a mass of trivial dreams which he explains according to Antiphon's rules of interpretation. The work, I admit, displays the acumen of its author, but it would have been better if he had cited illustrations of a more serious type.

At this point it is pertinent to mention Antiphon's well-known theory of the interpretation of dreams. His view is that the interpreters of dreams depend upon technical skill and not upon inspiration.

chunks.author: Antiphon the Sophist
chunks.text: Furthermore, is it not a fact that the conjectures of the interpreters of dreams give evidence of their authors' sagacity rather than afford any proof of a relation between dreams and the laws of nature? For example, a runner, who was planning to set out for the Olympic games, dreamed that he was riding in a chariot drawn by four horses. In the morning he went to consult an interpreter, who said to him, ‘You will win, for that is implied in the speed and strength of horses.’
chunks.credit: William Armistead Falconer · Cicero, De senectute, De amicitia, De divinatione, Loeb 154 (1923), De divinatione II.70.144, pp 531–533

chunks.author: Antiphon the Sophist
chunks.text: morning he went to consult an interpreter, who said to him, ‘You will win, for that is implied in the speed and strength of horses.’ Later the runner went to Antipho, who said, ‘You are bound to lose, for do you not see that four ran ahead of you?’ And behold another runner!—for the books of Chrysippus and Antipater are full of such dreams—but to return to the runner: he reported to an interpreter that he had dreamed of having been changed into an eagle.
chunks.credit: William Armistead Falconer · Cicero, De senectute, De amicitia, De divinatione, Loeb 154 (1923), De divinatione II.70.144, pp 531–533

The interpreter said to him, ‘You are the victor, for no bird flies faster than the eagle.’ This runner also consulted Antipho. ‘Simpleton,’ said the latter, ‘don't you see that you are beaten? For that bird is always pursuing and driving other birds before it and itself is always last.’

Teos brought forth, a source of pride to Greece,
The sweet Anacreon, who with sweet notes twined
A wreath of tuneful song in woman's praise,
The choicest ornament of revelling feasts,
The most seductive charm; a match for flutes'
Or pipes' shrill aid, or softly moving lyre:
O Teian bard, your fame shall never die;
Age shall not touch it; while the willing slave
Mingles the wine and water in the bowl,
And fills the welcome goblet for the guests;
While female hands, with many twinkling feet,
Lead their glad

chunks.text: Now the decree for his recall had been passed before this, on motion of Critias, the son of Callaeschrus, as Critias himself has written in his elegies, where he reminds Alcibiades of the favour in these words:— "Mine was the motion that brought thee back; I made it in public; Words and writing were mine; this the task I performed; Signet and seal of words that were mine give warrant as follows."
chunks.credit: Bernadotte Perrin · Plutarch, Lives, Loeb Classical Library (1916)

chunks.author: Critias
chunks.text:
By various passions are our lives engross’d;
One craves nobility, another cares not
For titles, but is anxious to be call’d
The founder of a wealthy house; he too
Who from his soul ne’er spoke an honest truth,
Delights by mere effrontery to persuade
All those around him; some at the expence
Of virtue seek base lucre; thus the life
Of man is all one error. But I wish
For nought beyond an honourable name.
chunks.credit: Michael Wodhull · The Nineteen Tragedies and Fragments of Euripides, translated by Michael Wodhull, second edition, vol. III (London: John Nichols and Son, 1809), p. 386, Rhadamanthus
